pr_title: Add analyzer for detecting misplaced attributes on delegates

issue_context.title: Detecting when attributes are put on a method called by a lambda instead of the lambda itself

review_comments:
This one's interesting - if the code looked like:

```C#
(int id) => if (id == 0) { return Results.NotFound(); } else { return Hello(); }
```

This would produce no diagnostics? Is that weird?

Yeah, that's a consequence of not doing the full search through the syntax tree that we were doing before (see https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/35779#discussion_r696849251).

Supporting this scenario invites the question of how "deep" in the syntax tree we want to look for returned invocations and support throwing a warning.

Yep, good idea. Here's the expected behavior for these:

1. Invalid reference: No warning from us but user gets a not defined warning.
2. Method reference: No warning from us since this warning only applies to lambdas.
3. Reference to a method in a different class: Warning from us about misplaced attribute.

> Where PersonHandlers.GetPersonId is in a separate source file / SyntaxTree

For this part, I couldn't find any examples in our codebase of the `GetDiagnosticsAsync` method processing sources from different source files so I put it in separate files. Is there a way to do that?
Shouldn't we be producing the diagnostic on the attribute (rather than on the delegate)?
Hmmm, I think it makes more sense to put it on the delegate since that is where the user will take the action to resolve the issue (absent us providing a codefix).

As I was reviewing this, I thought of at least one attribute you might want to use on your method - https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.diagnostics.codeanalysis.requiresunreferencedcodeattribute?view=net-5.0 to suppress linker warnings.
I was talking to @captainsafia about this and I think we could start by only warning for attributes that have known metadata. Ones in the Microsoft.AspNetCore namespace.

Yep -- we can limit this to only attributes defined in our namespace.

It also has the consequence of us throwing false-positives for compiler generated attributes and attributes that would intentionally be on the method as referenced above.
Do compiler generated attributes (e.g. [AsyncStateMachineAttribute]) appear in this list?

Yep, it will include compiler generated ones in the list. This is fixed though by incorporating the namespace check mentioned in https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/35779/files#r697101285. Added validation for this.

`IInvocationOperation` has a method symbol on it - https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.codeanalysis.operations.iinvocationoperation.targetmethod?view=roslyn-dotnet-3.11.0#Microsoft_CodeAnalysis_Operations_IInvocationOperation_TargetMethod. Is that different from this?

This will work for lambdas that are structured like `() => { return Hello(); }` but it won't work for ones that are structured like `() => Hello()`.

The reason being is that `() => Hello()` produces an operation structure that looks like this:

- AnonymousFunctionOperation
  - BlockOperation (Syntax: InvocationExpressions)

Whereas, the `() => { return Hello() }` syntax will produce:

- AnonymousFunctionOperation
  - BlockOperation
    - ReturnOperation
      - InvocationOperation

AKA, you can extract the `InvocationOperation` from a lambda that explicitly returns an invocation instead of calling it.

So, that's why I ended up converging on the `InvocationSyntax` since we could extract that from both forms.
